summary: Adds new values to the IANA registry of digest algorithms used by Instance Digests in HTTP, and updates earlier values. Instance digests provide a checksum of a whole representation of a resource. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A fingerprint on a downloaded file lets you check it is whole, and this adds more fingerprint methods to the list.

questions: which hash algorithms for http digest
how does http verify downloaded files
subtitle: Adding SHA-256 and SHA-512 to the list of checksums for HTTP files

tldr.problem: HTTP lets you download a file with a checksum so you can verify it was not corrupted or tampered with, but the registry of which hash algorithms are allowed was outdated and missing modern algorithms.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5843 updates the IANA registry of digest algorithms used by HTTP Instance Digests, adds SHA-256 and SHA-512, and updates the references for existing entries (MD5 and SHA-1).
tldr.outcome: HTTP clients and servers can now use stronger hash algorithms to verify file integrity, improving security for downloads.

today: RFC 5843 remains valid. SHA-256 and SHA-512 are now standard options in the IANA registry. Modern browsers and HTTP libraries use these algorithms for file integrity verification. MD5 and SHA-1 are deprecated for security-critical uses but remain in the registry for compatibility.

sections.title: Instance Digests in HTTP
sections.content: Instance Digest is an HTTP feature (defined in RFC 3230 in 2002) that lets a server provide a checksum—also called a digest or hash—of a file it is sending. The client receives both the file and its digest and can verify that the file has not been corrupted in transit or tampered with. The digest is computed using a hash algorithm like MD5 or SHA-1. IANA maintains a registry of which algorithms are acceptable. By 2010, the registry was outdated and missing stronger algorithms like SHA-256 and SHA-512. Note that this is different from HTTP Digest Authentication, which is a login mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The server gives you a file and a fingerprint. You check if the fingerprint matches. If it does, the file is good.

sections.title: Updated and New Algorithms
sections.content: RFC 5843 updates the registry entries for MD5 and SHA (SHA-1), clarifying that the output is encoded using base64 and citing the correct modern references. It then adds two new entries: SHA-256 and SHA-512, both from the FIPS 180-3 standard. Each new entry includes its description, how the output is encoded (base64), and its references. An example in the RFC shows a SHA-256 digest: 'SHA-256=MWVkMWQxYTRiMzk5MDQ0MzI3NGU5NDEyZTk5OWY1ZGFmNzgyZTJlODYzYjRjYzFhOTlmNTQwYzI2M2QwM2U2MQ=='.
sections.plainLanguage: Stronger fingerprint methods like SHA-256 can now be used instead of the older MD5 and SHA-1, making verification more secure.

sections.title: Practical Benefit
sections.content: By adding SHA-256 and SHA-512 to the registry, the RFC allows HTTP implementations to use stronger, more modern cryptographic hash functions. This is important because MD5 and SHA-1 have known weaknesses and are no longer recommended for security-critical applications. SHA-256 and SHA-512 are part of the SHA-2 family and are widely trusted. HTTP clients and servers can now securely verify large downloads and critical files using modern algorithms without needing proprietary extensions or workarounds.
sections.plainLanguage: Now the Internet can use better fingerprinting methods that are harder to fake or break, making file downloads more trustworthy.
